problem.title_as_question: Why does your forehand keep disappearing, and how do you fix it?
problem.definition: The forehand stroke loses control, repeatability, and consistency because players lack proximal stability in the hip-trunk connection and back-shoulder attachment, leading to upper body compensations and mistimed arm swings.
prerequisites: Players seeking a stable, repeatable forehand foundation who tend to pop up, over-rotate, or lose ball control when trying to accelerate.

symptoms.description: Torso pops straight up and over-rotates instead of pulsing rotation smoothly into the ball.
Balls spray long (e.g., hitting the back fence) or shank even at slow swing speeds.
Hitting arm feels disconnected, crashing into the trunk, or moving wildly out of control.
Player fails to finish balanced over the front foot, instead falling backward, left, or right.
Racket micro-twists or slips in the palm before or during contact.

causes.statement: Hip-trunk instability caused by straight or forward-thrusting hips and knees-forward, quad-dominant posture.
Intentionally driving or popping the pelvis forward rather than rotating the upper body over anchored hips.
Loading onto the inside flat foot or heel rather than loading the arch and outside ball of the foot.
Lack of shoulder attachment to the torso due to upper trap shrugging and inactivated mid-traps/serratus.
Improper lateral spacing, crowding the contact point and blocking the natural swinging lane.
Excessively loose grip tension, gaps between hand and grip, or a slipping handle preventing racket perception.

solutions.summary: Sideways Pelvis Rotation Drill: Set hips sideways and focus entirely on rotating the upper body over the hips without intentionally thrusting the pelvis forward.
Romanian Deadlift Hinge Drill: Hit balls while exaggerating butt back, chest forward, and knees relatively straight to turn off quads and force hip hinge activation.
Foot Arch Loading Test: Roll knee and pressure across the ball of the foot to load the arch and outer ball of the foot rather than collapsing onto the inside.
Front Foot Balanced Finish: Glide weight through contact and hold a completely stable finish balanced over the front foot without falling off.
Back Shoulder Attachment Prep: Consciously undo any upper trap shrugging, drawing the shoulder down and activating mid-traps and serratus with isometric tone.
Lateral Swinging Lane Spacing: Position the body to keep the ball noticeably farther away laterally to allow the racket to swing through the natural lane.
solutions.external_goal: Keep the ball pushed farther away to the side

solutions.summary: Grip Seating and Firmness Check: Push handle deep into the palm/V with the opposite hand, remove all gaps, and maintain 5-6/10 tension to prevent micro-slipping.
solutions.external_goal: Push racket handle firmly into the palm with the non-dominant hand
